item.title: Why Must Artists Starve?
item.description: Why is it greedy for creatives to expect to be paid for their work, instead of begging for optional tips?
item.content:encoded:
Today, I’m writing about writing, which I don’t do often but it felt necessary. If that’s not your thing, stay tuned for tomorrow when I will cover the “epidemic” of women demanding men call Ubers for them on first dates.

In a semi-recent Note, I told the true story of my six-year-old son asking me to stop doing my work so I could play with him. (Before you call me a monster, we don’t have any childcare in the summers, so sometimes I have to finish up some work while my kids entertain themselves. The horror, I know.) Anyway, I informed him that I was working but I’d be done in five minutes. He glanced over at my screen and said, “You’re not working, you’re writing. Nobody would pay someone for that.”

He’s six, so it’s cute. But he embodies a mindset held by many adults—many of whom are writers themselves.

A recent, extremely viral, short article asserts that Substack is collapsing, and the reason being, of course, is subscription fatigue. Substack has gotten too crowded, people are paying for too many subscriptions (“it’s impossible to support hundreds of writers!” the comments complain) sponsored content may be the future of this place, and so on and so forth. I’m not going to spend a long time debating this particular article, because the article was fine even if I don’t agree with all of it. Yes, Substack can be winner-take-all, but Substack is less winner-take-all than the literary industry, where even most bestselling authors will never be able to make a living off their books alone and any aspiring writers are beholden to nonsensical gatekeeping. But no, the article didn’t piss me off. What did piss me off were some of the top comments, which declared that independent writers, or any writers at all, should never charge a fixed price for their work:

From one of the top comments:

Most people around the world and throughout history have been perfectly happy with taking up collections, voluntary contributions, or busking as a means to patronize creative work they enjoy. These methods offer the consumer an opportunity to sample the product in some way, and decide to contribute, or not.

Similar comments complained about any sort of pricing or paywalls for any written content, whether on Substack or The New York Times, because writers should simply take joy in reaching an audience, any audience, and money should be a fun little afterthought. The argument wasn’t just that it wasn’t feasible for them to pay for a subscription, but that it was morally wrong for anyone to charge for one. As they put it, customers should be able to “sample” the work for free (and you can, it’s called the seven day free trial, Bucko!) but also, this sampling should be able to go on indefinitely. Writers (unlike anyone else in any other job) should simply beg for tips if they need the money so badly—and only the bare minimum to survive. Anything more is too greedy.

While I don’t read my own unsubscribes anymore (the last one I read, as I recall, just said, “fuck you,” and honestly, no notes) I recall an unsub I received a while back, which stated that they had initially wanted to “support” me, but had unsubscribed because I had recently gone on a family vacation and therefore I “clearly didn’t need it.”

There’s just one problem (well, many problems, but we’ll get to that.) My paywalls—and those of other people who do this full-time—are a fair price for a product. They are not charity. I am not asking anyone to support me because I “need the money,” any more than any person in any job needs the money. Pity is not a business model. I’m providing a service, and I hope that people pay for that service if they enjoy it. In my case, that service is 4-5 weekly articles on a variety of topics, and over 600 completed articles in archive, usually related to social dynamics but occasionally gorillas who can’t get laid (I guess that’s still social dynamics—and that one is free, by the way.) And while I’m not everyone’s cup of tea, I’m clearly right for some people.

I put this into practice myself as a reader too. I pay for several Substacks—not hundreds (who, aside from Chris Best himself, is a paid subscriber to hundreds? This is only something that happens if you feel morally obligated to subscribe to everyone who’s ever interacted with you) but about ten—not because I want to provide some sort of creative mutual aid, but because I like their work and find that paying for it is good value for what I am getting. If I’m going to subscribe to a Substack, it’s not because they have secret information I can’t find anywhere else, but because they have consistently interesting, frequent articles that I can enjoy while waiting in line for something as opposed to scrolling various brain-rotting feeds. It’s not about these writers needing me to survive. I am under no delusion that Matt Yglesias would be an unhoused body if not for my $80 annual donation.

Subscribe now

(Of course, it’s fine to remain a free subscriber! I am a free subscriber to many publications. I write free stuff too, and sometimes un-paywall articles for free subscribers. But even then, it’s not about whether I need to be “supported,” it’s about whether you want to pay for the full, high volume of my work or not.)

Why is writing considered the one profession where making money is questionable or “asking too much,” where you’re expected to make only enough money to survive, if anything at all? Or in the case of the noble buskers of yore, perhaps writers are meant to live on the street, occasionally going into Times Square to recite their latest essay on the commodification of girlhood.

Why is “being financially successful if you’re at the top of your field” an accepted outcome for every career except writers?

Imagine if this standard was applied to other professions. The average major league athlete makes millions of dollars a year, sometimes tens of millions of dollars. Even rookies make about as much as the most successful Substackers, on par with Noah Smith or Matt Yglesias, perhaps even as much as Heather Cox Richardson depending on the sport. And yet, you don’t hear many people saying that they will no longer pay for NBA League Pass because Donovan Mitchell’s new contract is nearing $70 million and he “doesn’t need the money.” You don’t hear anyone saying he’s grifting or greedy for making so much money off something—playing sports—that other people do for free. You don’t hear anyone saying, “People throughout history have been happy to play sports for mere fulfillment without all this money-grubbing! Why don’t NBA players just play basketball for fun and let us watch? Why must people pay for the supposed privilege to watch people play sports? I play sports for free on the weekends and I love it, and I’d be thrilled if people watched! Why won’t Donovan Mitchell do that?”

(Okay, yes, my husband helped me with this bit but I maintain I did know who Donovan Mitchell was before asking him about his salary or the pricing structure for NBA League Pass.)

Far be it from me to compare myself to Donovan Mitchell. Far be it from me, quite frankly, to even compare Heather Cox Richardson to Donovan Mitchell. But if people think it’s crazy, greedy or just plain unnecessary for Heather Cox Richardson to make a salary in the low seven figures, why is a high eight-figure salary completely reasonable for Donovan Mitchell? Neither of them are scamming—whether you like what they do or not, you are getting exactly the type of content you paid for. So why is a paywall a problem, but NBA League Pass isn’t? Like her or not, Heather Cox Richardson is providing a service that other writers are simply not providing at the same consistency and quality, and that is why people pay for her but will not pay for other writers. There is a reason people will pay to watch their favorite NBA team but will not pay to watch a bunch of neighborhood dads play basketball at the park. This doesn’t mean that writing or basketball games should always be free, or that HCR or Donovan Mitchell are getting away with a scam. Only that, when most people do write or play basketball, it’s a hobby, not a profession. It’s still a profession for some, and those people get paid.

I’m aware NBA League Pass is not the exact same pricing model as a subscription to a Substack, but also, Donovan Mitchell makes significantly more money than even the most successful Substackers. Surely, there is a (bad) argument to be made that NBA League Pass is money-grubbing because “they don’t need more money.” They may not, but you want to watch NBA, so you pay for it!

That’s the only way you can look at Substack—paying for something you enjoy reading which provides some degree of entertainment or informational value, full stop. If you look at Substack subscriptions like a variety of “help me get out of my toxic roommate situation” GoFundMe’s, then of course you’ll be subscribed to too many, not find them worth it, and eventually feel that paywalls are a scam if it turns out the writer is not eating cat food for lunch every day. That should never be your motivation to pay for a subscription in the first place!

You might be tempted to assume that people who take issue with paywalls are anti-creative, anti-intellectual jerks who couldn’t possibly understand the value of the written word. And yet! I’ve noticed that people who find paywalls absurd or corrupt are often people who are writers themselves or people who fancy themselves particularly literary and refined. This may sound surprising, but it isn’t. These are people who enjoy writing, but whose full-time job is something else. Maybe they work in academia, maybe they work in tech, maybe they have a wealthier spouse or family who is supporting their writing for which they aren’t paid, but they do not rely on a salary for their writing (at least not on Substack) because being a salaried writer is just not very common.

Another comment says:

I don’t even try and charge for a sub. Support me by buying my books.

Okay, well, your business model is writing books and having people pay for them. Of course you’re not trying to charge people for subscriptions—you’re making money off your books! A feat, by the way, which most successful Substack writers can’t hack. Although if I ever do get published, I’m tempted to say, “Just take my book for free and subscribe to my Substack! I would never even try to charge someone for my book!”

Many of the most anti-paid-writer voices in the comments section were hobby writers whom nobody was paying. Well, okay. Again, I get it, I’ve not only been there but I was Mayor of There for fifteen years of writing comedic memoirs that I could barely convince my own family members to read. The problem is that because writing is a thankless hobby for most people who do it, it’s very easy to insist that it should be a thankless hobby for everyone. I love sewing, and nobody pays me to sew (in fact, my husband can attest to the fact that I spend quite a bit of money sewing.) This does not mean, however, that professional fashion designers should simply offer their work for free. After all, I design children’s clothes constantly and nobody pays me!

Another reason why you shouldn’t take the “tip jar” approach to your writing: unlike a regular paywall strategy, this only makes sense if you actually need the money! I think it’s far more duplicitous to beg for donations while not really needing the money, than to be upfront about the fact that your paywall represents your full-time job, no matter your person level of financial need. Personally, if I felt I had “donated” to a struggling writer and then I found out she was married to a corporate lawyer, I’d be a bit miffed, but I have no problem paying for a subscription for a talented and consistent writer, even if I already know they’re rich.

Obviously, I am biased here. Substack has worked out well for me (although I am no longer experiencing the growth that I saw earlier in my career—I expected I’d plateau at some point) but in general, I think their pricing model is fine. I’ve written before (yes, for free) about how “I just want to pay $1 per article” is a ridiculous idea that will turn Substack into a slop trough, perhaps in a best case scenario temporarily benefiting talented but less prolific writers, and ultimately driving full-time writers off the platform entirely. Often, the pipe dreams about how Substack should change are driven by people who A.) believe in a form of “anti-capitalism” wherein everyone gets really high-quality things for free or cheap all the time with no consideration to who is making the things (“Why can’t you find a high-quality natural fiber dress for $20? Capitalism strikes again!) or B.) are actively rooting against the platform because they thought it was a get rich quick scheme and it actually required a lot of hard work and more frustratingly, dumb luck.

Subscribe now

I want to be charitable toward the people in the second group, no matter how annoying they are, because they may have actually been misled. Substack, at times, has been presented as a get rich quick scheme. Throughout my time on this platform, I have seen countless posts from people of whom I’d never heard before, who supposedly earned untold riches from writing on Substack, but the only thing they write about is writing on Substack. It’s a classic MLM type scheme where the only thing they’re actually writing about is the making money, and the only thing they’re selling are instructions for making money, and they’re presenting such a moneymaking endeavor as much more accessible than it actually is. I assume that one of their “tips” for making money on Substack is to write about making money on Substack and sell those tips to other people who want to make money on Substack. I actually caught one of these grifters in a lie when she claimed she was raking in $100K annually on Substack but still only had the transparent orange checkmark next to her name—which means she had fewer than 1,000 paid subscribers. There are a bunch of people like this, and I put the blame partially at their feet for making it sound like anyone, no matter their degree of talent and consistency, can get rich on Substack. Of course, the platform will look like it’s failing if your initial assumption was that “anyone” could make six figures here doing nothing that actually stood out or required real work. Second, if this was your initial assumption, it must be a pretty big bummer when it doesn’t come to pass, especially if you’ve paid someone to help you learn these surefire “skills” to make it big.

Consider this, for a moment: Substack has been called “Onlyfans for intellectuals.” Onlyfans is still going strong. It’s just that the vast majority of performers on Onlyfans don’t make much money. I don’t want to debate sex work itself, but the problem isn’t how Onlyfans is structured, it’s the fact that many people believed that because some people make a lot of money on Onlyfans, anyone could.

I know Substack is not perfect. There are some great writers here, some not-so-great writers, and everything in between. Because there is so much diversity of writers, with people writing on basically every topic imaginable, you can easily curate just a few (3? 5? 9?) who suit your needs and provide a much more stimulating alternative to scrolling social media—a cost I think is worth it when you consider what you’d be doing with your time instead of reading thoughtful, funny or interesting articles. But you will never find yourself on a platform full of high-quality, ad-free content written by full-time writers, which you get for free.

Because nobody’s full-time job should be unpaid.

Subscribe now

item.title: Many Such Takes: Thanksgiving Canceled, Millennial Marriage, Pit Bulls (Again) and More
item.description: The most unhinged discourse of the week, always free
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to Many Such Takes, my twice-monthly roundup of Internet drama and discourse (mostly Twitter) and funny happenings online. If you enjoy a good guilty pleasure of unhinged discourse, this is for you. If it’s not your kind of thing, I implore you to check out my other recent articles, because while publishing 4-5 times a week, there’s always something for someone:

  • Relationships: Why don’t women make the first move?

  • Social dynamics: Why I gave up on throwing big parties

  • Fashion: 21 Outfits I wore in Paris this July

  • Personal essay: My “secret club” at theater camp got me in a lot of trouble

  • Parenting: Is it “outsourcing” to occasionally get help with your kids?

  • More relationships: Is the stereotype of women being “clingy” about marriage and babies still true?

While MST will always be free, the rest of my content—4 articles per week—are paid. As I said before, it’s a little bit of everything—mostly social dynamics (dating, friendship, marriage, etc) but also some fashion, and some random shower thoughts questions like what happened to picky eaters in olden times? If that sounds appealing, consider becoming a paid subscriber. I’m running a 30% off sale on annual subscriptions for the next week! (Even at my regular prices, I have some of the lowest $-for-article volume pricing on Substack, but a summer sale can’t hurt.)

Get 30% off forever

Thanksgiving Canceled

Time for some good old fashioned Woke 1 discourse! Francesca Hong is a candidate running for governor of Wisconsin, and this week, some particularly memorable past moments of hers came to light. First, she previously described having a half-white son (who was presumably sired by the white guy she married) as an uncomfortable “proximity to whiteness.”

But most of the ire this week came from the fact that in 2020 (who amongst us was not a little insane in 2020) she proposed canceling Thanksgiving due to trauma imposed on indigenous “folx” by pilgrims who weren’t WEARING A FUCKING MASK:

I feel weird defending anything about this tweet, but considering it was 2020, “cancel Thanksgiving” likely didn’t mean getting rid of the holiday entirely, but staying home during that particular Thanksgiving. I’m sure many of you also think that’s stupid, but there is a meaningful difference between “canceling” in the covid sense, and cancellation.

But, as it turns out, she has ragged on basically every holiday, including a line about feeling “attacked” when non-consensually exposed to a Christmas-related imagery via a computer background:

So, how is she going to do damage control? During a relatively softball interview, she did a 180 and declared that while she is a bit of a “curmudgeon” about most holidays, her favorite holiday is Thanksgiving after all! Just say you hate indigenous folx and go. She then went on to very vaguely and oddly describe Thanksgiving in a way that only someone who never celebrated it would, summing it up as a “big event,” with very little detail indicating any real familiarity.

As I said, she talks about Thanksgiving the way Trump talks about the Bible.

More good takes:

Subscribe now

Millennial Marriage

I was happy to see this topic in the discourse because this had been my beat for ages now. Some of my fellow millennial women pointed out that conversations about women of their generation “delaying marriage” are incongruent with the experiences of secular millennial women in the 2000s and 2010s: being called crazy if you wanted any commitment at all, with the understanding that men didn’t want to be married and would put it off as long as possible. Now, suddenly, women have “delayed!”

While I’m sure some women deliberately deprioritized marriage to focus on other things, my anecdotal experience of being a millennial woman was that nearly every woman wanted marriage more than her boyfriend did (a lot of time, even admitting you wanted a monogamous boyfriend made you seem “crazy”) and that anti-marriage sentiment was popular among lots of young men, not just the ones with options.

I wrote about this exact phenomenon here

This (very apt) tweet seems to have started the discourse:

Followed by this one, which really kicked shit off:

I maintain Lisa is correct! At least where I grew up, it was considered “crazy” to even mention you wanted to get married at some point, even if you were well into your twenties! Dating for marriage was considered so unhinged and weird that you would have to pretend you weren’t doing it, even when dating relatively older guys. I had a male friend in his early thirties—not particularly Chadly or tall or good with women, just a regular guy—who stopped seeing a woman because she mentioned marriage too early on, even though it was more generally speaking and not about marrying him specifically. Another friend (age 38 at the time) advised my husband to never live with a woman or get married, right after we got engaged (nice.) Anyway, MANY SUCH CASES!

I will say the trend seems to be shifting a bit, and Gen Z men do seem a bit more interested in marriage than their female counterparts, although things probably haven’t changed as much as trad Twitter would have you think. More about that here:

Subscribe now

Primetime

In case you missed it, there’s a A24 new movie on the horizon—Primetime, based on the career of Chris Hansen of To Catch a Predator fame. Chris Hansen will be played by none other than Robert Pattinson who does a…fairly convincing Chris Hansen impression despite not looking very much like him.

But perhaps the best Primetime discourse came from this tweet, which takes issue with the fact that a talented actor fell so far that he was “forced” to play a pedophile:

I couldn’t help but feel I was getting shades of “Sydney Sweeney is a pedophile because she played a character who sucked on a binky during a sexy video in Euphoria.”

This sparked some pretty entertaining responses:

But perhaps the best tweet about this movie came from this person, with 81K likes and counting:

Subscribe now

Survyeys

I interrupt this programming to ask you to fill out my anonymous surveys!

Consider:

  • This one about socialization

  • This one about dating and politics

  • This one about first dates

Pit Bulls (Again)

I am obviously no stranger to “aggressive dog discourse.” I was never a big pit bull person, but also didn’t care that much either way. I thought about pit bulls about as much as I thought about the Steelers, which is to say, almost never. If the topic came up, I mostly bought into the “it’s the owner, not the dog” thing because it was the line that was parroted around me constantly, and I even had people telling me it was racist—not dog-racist, but like, actually racist, somehow, to believe dog breeds had any inherently different traits despite being bred specifically for different traits, unlike humans.

Until I had kids. Suddenly, there were a bunch of pit bulls (often unleashed!) roaming around my neighborhood, and I was increasingly aware of just how badly that can go when little kids are involved. My husband was chased and nearly bitten by one on his run, and when he yelled at the owner for losing control of her dog, she burst into tears and was comforted by bystanders who thought my husband was a big ol’ meanie. Frequently, I cross the street to get away from one, and its owner yells after me that “she’s friendly,” as if I’m supposed to know that (or believe them, which, I don’t.) I’ve seen stories of pit bulls with aggressive histories erased and pushed onto families, only to kill their children. I’m aware that shelters are passing off pit bulls as other breeds to sanitize them for families who otherwise may have safety concerns. Consider me radicalized.

Now, I’m at the point where I view pit bulls more or less as domesticated tigers or assault rifles with their own free will, carrying a small chance they will randomly just snap and kill someone for no reason. Because, well, they sometimes do that, even when they’re raised by attentive, loving suburban families who would never abuse an animal. So much for “the owner.” As for chihuahuas being more aggressive, they have yet to kill anyone!

All that to say, this is basically the only Twitter hivemind topics where I think Twitter is much more sane and reasonable than the general population, who mostly, across political lines, believe that pit bulls are totally fine to allow around children because they have one and hasn’t eaten anyone yet. Well, pediatricians apparently disagree. But that doesn’t matter. Outside of Twitter, people think it’s crazy to be concerned about having your children around these things.

In case that rant somehow wasn’t enough for you, you can read more of my thoughts on the topic here.

But anyway, pit bulls are back in the Twitter discourse, because why not! They seem to connect everyone across the political spectrum, not easy to do on a place like X The Everything App, where nearly any position on any topic can have you hounded by people who are one crashout away from being sectioned.

I’ve rounded up some of the most insane/amusing takes, such as this guy who suggests that a child fleeing a pit bull should simply learn to stop being so afraid and the dog is only aggressively chasing them because they can smell fear (if this were true—and it may very well be—it’s an unintentionally great argument for “pit bulls are unsafe around children.”)

I can’t stop thinking about Crazy Zeke:

This one might take the cake for “bad takes:” If you live near a wacko who lets their pit bull roam free, the onus should be on you and your children to shelter in place indefinitely:

This is why I come to Twitter:

Anyway, because this invariably always comes back to “Other things are more dangerous” (and, based on deaths alone, yes) I will just leave this here:

I loled:

Funny Tweets/Other Happenings

For a while this particular video of a contestant from the TLC show, Match Me Abroad, was going viral on Twitter. I guarantee you that it goes in a very different direction than you’re expecting:

A good old fashioned parenting tweet:

Monitoring this situation:

And, last but not least, a “we should go to war” post from a man who is living in a country that is involved in wars, has an army, and has suspiciously not joined said army. Apparently, billions must die because of…*checks notes* too many men being stay-at-home boyfriends.

item.title: In Defense of Silly Little Rules
item.description: How I was radicalized by the bedlam of Disneyland
item.content:encoded:
This article is free, but most of my 4-5 weekly articles are paid, so consider becoming a free or paid subscriber if you enjoy it!

This summer, my husband and I took our kids to Disneyland Paris. It was my first Disney trip since a Los Angeles family trip when I was twelve, when the caricature artist painted a comically enormous chin on me, only to revise it after my mom whispered, “That’s an insecurity of hers,” to him.

But anyway.

Disneyland Paris is not as intense as Disneyworld in Orlando (where I’ve actually never been, I’m a bit scared.) Disneyland Paris is much smaller, much cheaper, and it’s a day trip because you can get there on a forty-minute train, provided you are in Paris to begin with. (I am aware at this point, someone might say something like, “Wow, real OUT OF TOUCH, assuming EVERYONE is always in Paris.” Privilege checked!)

But one thing about Disneyland Paris which is the same as any Disney location? There is a lot of waiting. And not just waiting—waiting with children who don’t always understand why they have to wait. We took an early morning train so we would arrive before it opened, figuring this was our only chance to take our daughter on the very popular Frozen ride. The wait time for that ride was already over an hour before the park opened. So with this reality check in mind, we expected to wait a lot, and warned our kids that being bored in line was the price they’d pay for fun rides. Our kids whined a little, but complied.

But you know who didn’t comply? Certain poorly-behaved adults.

As we waited at the front gates for the park to open (at which point we could swipe our tickets and start waiting for rides) we noticed that everyone was basically cooperating, fully aware that waiting was part of the deal, except for four adults in their twenties wearing Mickey Mouse ears and backpacks, who frantically scampered past the line, giggling. They were convinced that they had figured out the “one secret trick” to avoiding the wait times at Disney—just break the rules, while hoping everyone else follows them.

Nobody did anything about it. They had cut a bunch of families, for the most part, and none of us were looking to brawl—or worse, be a Karen. They cut everyone, probably entered the ride lines before everyone else, and did the whole thing without a hint of shame.

Later, when we were waiting for a ride, we noticed there was a single rider line, where people riding alone could fill spare spots and enjoy shorter wait times. My husband noticed four young women pretending not to know each other in the line, then laughing and performing a taunting dance together when the ride attendants weren’t looking, basking in the victory of having fooled them. Immediately, the attendant noticed what they were doing and kicked them out of the line. The same thing happened with two other adults who had been pretending to be unacquainted. Finally, a third man excused himself from the line and admitted that he and his friends were also taking advantage of the single rider line but he’d rather not suffer the indignity of being found out and ejected.

Subscribe now

Obviously, none of this is a big deal. Despite what some on Bluesky might insist, I am not advocating that these people be drawn and quartered in the town square. But they activated a very particular pet peeve of mine, which is that even when rules seem small and inconsequential, breaking them for pure selfishness doesn’t only imply that the rule-breaker don’t care about the rules. It implies that they still want to enjoy a society where everyone else follows the rules, but they don’t, because they are special. And unlike fare evasion or shoplifting, these people cannot claim, even insincerely, that financial hardship or a rebellion against capitalism, AI, or Jeff Bezos was at the heart of their decision. They were at Disneyland!

I would argue, as I have before, that most people who evade fare or shoplift are also not doing it because they must steal to survive. Not to beat a dead stolen lemon, but when well-off writer Jia Tolentino notoriously joked about shoplifting a couple lemons from Whole Foods and people responded by confronting her outside her home, I thought that was a bit much. It was, after all, just lemons. But this behavior pissed people off (even if they went too far) precisely because Jia Tolentino (and other upper middle class people who steal for thrills, convenience, or for political statements) are not only stealing, but benefiting from a society where most people don’t steal. If literally every customer stole from Whole Foods instead of paying, there would simply be no Whole Foods, or the security would ramp up significantly to the point that shopping there would be very unpleasant (see: everything now locked up at CVS after people decided the rules didn’t apply to them). In that same interview, Hasan Piker defended shoplifting by pointing out that a certain amount of loss is baked into these businesses’ pricing model. That may be true, but it still assumes that only certain people will shoplifting. Why do you deserve to be in that subset but everyone else doesn’t?

The same is true, quite frankly, of Disney. Sure, things will not fall apart if only some people cut the lines. But why do you get to be one of those people?

Perhaps some rules are unnecessary and meant to be broken, but generally a good litmus test is: if everyone broke this rule, what would happen? Most of the time, you’ll find that if everyone broke a rule you’d like to break, the location where the rule-breaking took place would become completely unusable and descend into full CHAZ-tier anarchy. True, throwing a soda can on the ground should not earn you prison time, but if everyone littered all the time, the streets would be a disaster. Anyone who frequently litters has not just ignored a rule. They have decided that they are special and this rule doesn’t apply to them, but should still apply to everyone else (because surely, they don’t want to wade through two feet of empty hot Cheetos bags every day.)

The dog owner who proudly walks around town with an unleashed and aggressive dog is just taking a bet that other people will leash their own aggressive dogs, who might otherwise pose a danger to his. (And don’t get me started on the copious dog shit everywhere—I’m sure the people who allowed their dog to leave it are still very happy that other people are not smearing dog poop everywhere.) The person taking up two parking spots with her car has benefited from a parking space where everyone else only took up one. Sure, none of this should be jailable, but certainly we must do something. Genuinely, bring back this:

People who break these “minor” rules are essentially the same people who refused to do any work for their school projects, but still got to enjoy a good grade because the nerds stepped in and finished it for them. Most of society does not want bedlam; they will follow the rules even if other people don’t. But it doesn’t take many people to completely ruin an experience for the rule-followers.

I can’t help but notice that public spaces are made less convenient, less safe and less enjoyable because of selfish rule-breakers, or measures taken specifically to deter selfish rule-breakers. Thought you could enjoy the pretty fountain at the park? Well, you can’t, because someone threw garbage in the water and now it’s being drained for cleaning. Thought you could enjoy the donated plastic Barbie van at the park with your children? Well, you can’t, because someone lit it on fire and it melted onto the slide in spiky fragments, making the entire play structure unsafe until the city can come to fix it (yes, this actually happened near me a few years ago.) Oh, someone donated a little Fisher Price plastic food truck to the playground, so cute! Oh wait, a bunch of teenagers stomped on it overnight and now the park is littered in broken pieces of plastic. You thought you could enjoy a walk outside with your baby? Well, despite the “NO DOGS” sign, someone has shown up with his traumatized rescue pit bull who is “oh so friendly” and doesn’t need a leash.

It’s easy to call people like me crotchety Squidwards, but it doesn’t take that many people to devolve a society into a place where everything is filthy, unusable, unsafe or just unpleasant. Demonizing anyone (especially a woman) who stands up for these rules as a “Karen” has backfired, as now the Mrs. Crumplebottom elders of society who used to unofficially keep everyone in line by wagging their fingers at rule-breakers are too afraid to be recorded out of context. Assuming that anyone who breaks these rules is just poor has also backfired, since it’s abundantly clear that plenty of people break the rules for reasons that have nothing to do with financial hardship. The chess park is dead, the mural is vandalized, the playground is unusable, dog shit is all over the streets, adults are cutting children at Disneyland, but hey…at least the rule-breakers don’t have to be inconvenienced.
